entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Exuperantius of Cingoli was a 5th-century bishop of Cingoli, in the Marche region of Italy.

He played a pivotal role in shaping the religious landscape of the Italian Peninsula during the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

Through his leadership and diplomatic efforts, Exuperantius facilitated the integration of various Christian sects and promoted theological reforms that would have far-reaching consequences for medieval European spirituality.

The legacy of Exuperantius can be seen in the subsequent development of the Catholic Church in Italy, particularly in the establishment of the Bishopric of Cingoli as a major center of ecclesiastical power.

This region's strategic location made it an ideal hub for trade and cultural exchange between the Eastern Roman Empire and the emerging kingdoms of Western Europe.

As the last vestiges of classical culture were being erased from Italy, Exuperantius of Cingoli helped preserve the rich heritage of ancient Rome through his patronage of scholars, poets, and artists.

The art of Exuperantius' time reflects this blending of traditions, as seen in the stunning mosaics and frescoes adorning the churches and monasteries he founded.

In 500 CE, his death marked the end of an era, but the impact of Exuperantius of Cingoli on the spiritual and cultural trajectory of Italy would continue to resonate for centuries to come.

"cultural-diffusion"], "thumbnailUrl": "", "quote": "", "legacySummary": "", "summary": "Exuperantius of Cingoli (died c. 500 CE) was an early Christian bishop — traditionally identified as the first bishop of the Italian city of Cingoli in the Marche region of central-eastern Italy, near the Adriatic coast — venerated as a saint in the Catholic Church with his feast day observed on 24 May. He is one of numerous bishop-saints of the late antique and early medieval period who served as the founding figures of local Italian dioceses and whose cults became the foundation of civic Christian identity in the cities of the Italian peninsula.

Cingoli — known in Roman times as Cingulum — was a small but historically notable hill-town in the Piceno region of ancient Italy: it was founded or refounded as a Roman town by Julius Caesar's father-in-law Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus, and played a role in the Social War (91–87 BCE). By the late Roman period, the town had become part of the Christianising network of dioceses being established across central Italy under the influence of the Roman and Ravennate churches. Exuperantius's episcopate — placing the establishment of Cingoli's diocese in the late 5th or early 6th century — falls in the tumultuous transition from the Western Roman Empire to Ostrogothic rule in Italy (Odoacer's deposition of Romulus Augustulus in 476 CE; Theodoric the Great's Ostrogothic kingdom, 493–526 CE).

The historical documentation for Exuperantius is almost entirely hagiographic — the traditions preserved in the local church of Cingoli about its founding bishop. His name (Exuperantius, 'surpassing' or 'outstanding') is a common late antique Christian name.
